findings.title: Per-agent `Force` protocol has no consumer and contradicts the tick signature
findings.description: The `Force` (per-agent) protocol is described as "used for testing, reference implementations", but `tick()` accepts only `forces: list[BulkForce]` (see the Tick Function Signature section) — there is no path by which tick consumes a `Force`. The same section then says "The tick loop prefers the bulk variant when available", implying tick accepts both variants, which the signature does not. Finally, the Technical Requirements demand that "Placeholder forces exercise both the `Force` and `BulkForce` protocol paths" — unimplementable through the only entry point that exercises the pipeline. This is both an internal contradiction and a proportionality issue: two force protocols where one meets the requirement. Either give `Force` a defined consumer (e.g., an adapter to `BulkForce`, or a `forces: list[Force | BulkForce]` signature with documented dispatch) or cut the per-agent protocol and its placeholder from this slice.

findings.title: `query_radius` result ordering is unspecified, but slice 105 requires identical behavioral output after the swap
findings.description: The `SpatialQuery.query_radius` contract states only set semantics ("indices of all agents within radius"). The slice plan requires slice 105 to "Validate that behavioral output is identical before and after the swap (determinism preserved)". Force accumulation sums over neighbor lists; floating-point summation is order-sensitive, and a spatial hash returns neighbors in bucket order while brute force will naturally return index order — so the same neighbor set in different orders can produce bitwise-different forces, breaking 105's regression criterion. The interface contract should specify deterministic ordering (e.g., ascending index order) or explicitly declare forces order-independent and require implementations to enforce it, plus tie semantics for agents exactly at `radius`. This is a hidden dependency of the (105) integration point on an unstated contract term.

findings.title: Efficiency NFR is not restated with its target; "hundreds-of-agents scale" sits unreconciled against it
findings.description: The parent architecture states the NFR: "Support tens of thousands of agents at full behavioral fidelity on a single CPU process". This slice owns the tick hot loop — the path that NFR governs — but never restates the target. Instead the Spatial Query Protocol section asserts "acceptable for the hundreds-of-agents scale this slice targets", with no note that the tens-of-thousands target is deferred to slice 105. The vectorization requirement ("No Python-level per-agent loops in the hot path") is the right structural constraint but is not a substitute for the stated target. Restate the NFR with the specific target (tens of thousands of agents, single CPU process, full behavioral fidelity) and explicitly record that the brute-force spatial query is the known gap, closed by (105) — so a future reader doesn't mistake "hundreds of agents" for the engine's ceiling.

findings.title: Serialization-boundary ownership contradicts the parent architecture
findings.description: The architecture's "State serialization boundary" consideration states the engine "should define its internal precision **and provide an efficient conversion path at the serialization boundary**". The slice defines internal precision (float64) but flatly asserts the opposite ownership: "Float32 serialization conversion — serialization boundary is a world server concern" (Excluded) and "that conversion happens at the serialization boundary owned by the world server, not here." Deferring the *work* out of slice 100 is fine — the plan entry doesn't assign it here — but the doc should not decree a layer-ownership decision that reverses a stated architectural responsibility. Either the engine provides a zero-copy/efficient float32 export path (per the architecture) or this doc should flag the deviation for resolution when the world-server integration slices are defined, rather than asserting the world server owns it.

findings.title: Data Flow and Force Protocol sections contradict the "inactive agents unchanged" success criterion
findings.description: Data Flow step 5 and the Integration section state integration "applied to active agents only ... via NumPy fancy indexing", and the success criteria require "all others are unchanged". But the Force Protocol section justifies the full-population `BulkForce` return shape with: "this keeps the integration step simple (add force to velocity for all, but only active agents have non-zero forces)". Following that parenthetical means the velocity clamp (`clamp(velocity_new, max_speed)`) is also applied to all rows — which mutates inactive agents whenever an inactive agent's speed exceeds `max_speed` (e.g., at initialization or after a profile edit), silently violating the success criterion. Resolve the contradiction: either state unambiguously that all integration and clamping steps touch only `active_indices` rows (and drop the "add force for all" rationale), or document why clamping inactive rows is safe.

findings.title: `accelerations` array is beyond the plan's enumerated state and its lifecycle is undocumented
findings.description: The slice plan enumerates agent state as "positions, velocities, profile indices"; `AgentState` adds `accelerations` (N×2 float64). The State Management section lists it, but the Data Flow never says where per-tick force sums are accumulated — `accelerations` is the implied buffer, yet nothing states whether it is zeroed each tick or persists across ticks. If it persists, it is stale state the architecture's "engine is stateless between ticks" claim doesn't account for; if it's per-tick scratch, it arguably belongs in the tick loop rather than in the persistent state container. Either document it as the per-tick force accumulator (reset at tick start) or drop the field in favor of a local array.
